title: Count to two hundred
goal: Count, read, write and order numbers to 200.
look: Musa labels seed packets for a class project. What comes after ninety-nine?
learn: After 99 comes 100. Ten tens make one hundred. Count 98, 99, 100, 101, 102. Count in tens from 100 to 200.
worked: 136 means 1 hundred, 3 tens and 6 ones. 200 means 2 hundreds and no tens or ones.
play: Make a track from 90 to 110 on scrap paper. A partner covers a number. Name it and explain. Then use place-value cards to show numbers to 200.
hint: Use ten ten-bundles for a hundred before formal hundreds notation.

questions.prompt: Write one hundred and twenty-four in digits.
Show 172 as hundreds, tens and ones.

questions.answer: It has no tens between its hundred and eight ones.

title: Halves and quarters of sets
goal: Find one half, one quarter and three quarters.
look: Amina shares tops equally among teams. What makes sharing fair?
learn: To find half, share equally into 2 groups. To find a quarter, share equally into 4 groups. Three quarters means take 3 of those 4 equal groups.
worked: 12 tops make 4 equal groups of 3. One quarter of 12 is 3. Three quarters of 12 is 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
play: Share 8 then 12 tops into two and four equal groups. Point to one half, one quarter and three quarters. Label fractions on folded paper too.
hint: The denominator counts equal groups, not objects in one group.

questions.prompt: Draw four groups of 2 dots. Ring three groups. How many ringed dots?

questions.answer: Share into four groups of 3 and take three groups, giving 9.

title: Add without exchanging
goal: Add two- and three-digit numbers without regrouping.
look: Zainab counts books on two shelves. How can columns keep the totals clear?
learn: Line up hundreds, tens and ones. Add each column. No exchange is needed when each column total is below ten. Estimate first by considering the tens.
worked: 123 + 45: ones 3 + 5 = 8; tens 2 + 4 = 6; one hundred stays. Total 168.
play: Use place-value mats to add two numbers without an exchange. Start with totals below 200. Then try 123 + 214 = 337 with three-digit addends.
hint: A shorter number needs an empty hundreds place, not a shift into another column.

questions.prompt: 43 books and 24 books make how many?

questions.answer: 3 ones plus 5 ones make 8; no exchange is needed.

title: Make a new ten
goal: Add two-digit numbers with regrouping.
look: Musa counts 8 loose strips and 7 more. What happens when the ones reach ten?
learn: When there are 10 or more ones, exchange 10 ones for 1 ten. Write the remaining ones. Add the new ten to the tens column.
worked: 28 + 17: 8 + 7 = 15 ones = 1 ten and 5 ones. Tens: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Total 45. Check: 45 − 17 = 28.
play: Build 26 and 18 with paper bundles. Join, exchange ten loose strips for one bundle, and record 44.
hint: Say what is exchanged: ten ones for one ten. Keep the new ten visible.

questions.prompt: 18 tops and 15 more make how many?
Why does 8 + 7 give an extra ten?
questions.answer: 15 ones contain one group of ten and five ones left.

title: Add three amounts
goal: Add three numbers in stages and check.
look: Daniel records three teams’ points. Which two numbers could he add first?
learn: For three addends, add two first, then the third. Choose an easy pair. Keep every amount in the calculation exactly once.
worked: 18 + 12 + 7: first make 30, then 37. Check another order: 12 + 7 = 19; 19 + 18 = 37.
play: Draw three number cards. Build the total with place-value strips. Ask a partner to check in a different order.
hint: Choosing pairs can ease mental work; never omit the third addend.

questions.answer: 27 and 3 make 30, then add 6 to get 36.

title: Subtract tens and ones
goal: Subtract two-digit numbers without regrouping.
look: There are 58 paper strips. Amina uses 23. How can she separate tens and ones?
learn: Align place-value columns. Subtract ones from ones and tens from tens. Check by adding the difference to the amount removed.
play: Make a stock of 47 strips. Remove 12 in bundles and loose ones. Show the remaining 35.
hint: Read the story before choosing an operation. Ask what remains and what was removed.

title: Exchange a ten to subtract
goal: Subtract two-digit numbers with regrouping.
look: Musa has 4 bundles and 2 loose strips. How can he remove 7 loose strips?
learn: Exchange one ten for ten ones. The total value stays the same. Subtract the ones, then the remaining tens.
worked: 42 − 17: rewrite 42 as 3 tens and 12 ones. 12 − 7 = 5; 3 tens − 1 ten = 2 tens. Answer 25. Check 25 + 17 = 42.
play: Build 53. Exchange a bundle and remove 28. Record the stages. Check remaining 25 and removed 28 total 53.
hint: Do not subtract the smaller digit from the larger regardless of its position.

questions.prompt: Why can 52 be 4 tens and 12 ones?
questions.answer: One of five tens becomes ten ones; total value stays 52.

title: Equal groups and multiplication
goal: Use repeated addition and multiplication notation.
look: Zainab puts equal numbers of tops on mats. How can she count equal groups?
learn: Equal groups have the same number in each. In this book 3 × 4 means 3 groups of 4: 4 + 4 + 4. The sign × means multiplied by. An array has equal rows and columns.
worked: 3 groups of 4 tops = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. So 3 × 4 = 12.
play: Make 2, 3, 4 or 5 equal groups. Write repeated addition and multiplication for each. Check by counting all objects.
hint: Keep group count and group size distinct in the story even when products match.

questions.prompt: 4 groups of 2 tops contain how many?
Draw 3 rows of 3 dots. How many?
Why is 2 + 3 + 2 not three equal groups?
questions.answer: One group has 3 and the others have 2.

title: Missing-number puzzles
goal: Find unknowns and explain simple number relationships.
look: Daniel writes a sentence with a blank. How can his friends prove an answer?
learn: Both sides of equals have the same value. Find a missing part with objects, counting or an inverse operation. Test the number in the original sentence.
play: Make a blank in a true sentence. Exchange puzzles with a partner. Describe the number relationship in words.
hint: Let pupils model a solution before explaining the symbols.

questions.answer: Put 25 in the blank and verify 25 − 9 = 16.

title: Money and fair exchange
goal: Name money uses and exchange equal values.
look: Amina makes a pretend shop. What could people use money for besides buying a toy?
learn: Money can buy goods and services, be saved or be given. Naira is written ₦. Our pretend cards show ₦1, ₦2, ₦5, ₦10 and ₦20. They model values, not current notes or coins.
worked: Two ₦5 cards equal ₦10. Four ₦5 cards equal ₦20.
play: Exchange paper value cards for equal totals. An adult may show genuine money and identify its value. Do not assume our value cards match issued denominations.
hint: Historical scope uses amounts to ₦20. No present-day price claim is made.

questions.answer: Buying goods or services, saving or giving.

questions.prompt: Why is ₦10 worth more than three ₦2 cards?

title: Our pretend shop
goal: Buy and give change within ₦20.
look: Zainab labels pretend items for role-play. Who should check the change?
learn: Add item values for the cost. Subtract cost from payment for change. Both buyer and seller check. All prices here are invented mathematical values.
worked: Pretend costs: a card ₦6 and a paper shape ₦4. Total ₦10. Pay ₦20: change ₦10. Check ₦10 + ₦10 = ₦20.
play: Use paper objects and value cards. Take turns as buyer and seller. Keep cost and payment at or below ₦20.
hint: Do not send pupils shopping for this task. Include oral or pointing roles.

questions.prompt: Two pretend items cost ₦8 each. Total?
How can a buyer check the ₦8 change after ₦12 cost?
questions.answer: Add ₦12 and ₦8 to get the ₦20 payment.

title: Why we need a metre
goal: Compare body units and recognise metres and centimetres.
look: Musa and Amina get different span counts for the same table. Could both be careful?
learn: Hand spans differ, so counts can differ. Standard units have agreed sizes. Metre is written m; centimetre is cm. 100 cm = 1 m. A ruler can measure short lengths; a metre strip measures longer ones.
worked: A 30 cm ruler is useful for a book. A metre strip is useful for a table or classroom distance.
play: Two pupils measure a table with their own spans. Compare counts. Then use the same ruler or metre strip and explain the results.
hint: Never use a scaled printed ruler diagram as a physical ruler.

questions.prompt: How many cm are in 1 m?
Choose a convenient unit for a pencil: cm or m.
Choose a convenient unit for classroom length: cm or m.
Measure a book with a real ruler. Record cm.
questions.answer: Practical reading with correct zero alignment and cm unit.
Different people’s spans can have different lengths.

title: Whole hours and half hours
goal: Read whole-hour and half-hour times.
look: Daniel looks at a clock. Which hand gives the minutes?
learn: The long hand shows minutes; the short hand hours. At a whole hour the minute hand is at 12. At half past it is at 6; the hour hand is halfway to the next hour.
worked: At 3:00 the short hand points to 3 and the long hand to 12. At 3:30 the short hand is halfway between 3 and 4, with the long hand at 6.
play: Make a paper clock with movable hands. Show whole and half hours for a partner to name.
hint: Distinguish hand lengths. Move the hour hand between hour marks at half past.

questions.prompt: Write half past four in digits.
At 7:00 where is the minute hand?
At 9:30 where is the minute hand?
Read clock A in the diagram.
Where is the hour hand at 2:30? Explain.
questions.answer: Halfway between 2 and 3, because half an hour has passed.

title: Seven days in a week
goal: Name and order weekdays.
look: The friends plan classroom jobs. How can they show which day follows another?
learn: The days in order here are Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. A week has 7 days. After Sunday comes Monday again.
worked: The day after Tuesday is Wednesday. The day before Monday is Sunday.
play: Make seven day cards. Put them in a circle and name the next day. This is a practice sequence, not a claim about every school timetable.
hint: Connect names to a real calendar. Respect different family routines.

questions.prompt: How many days make a week?
Today is Wednesday. What is tomorrow?

title: Order by weight
goal: Arrange objects from lightest to heaviest.
look: Amina compares a leaf, an eraser and a small stone. What evidence is needed?
learn: Compare pairs on a balance. Record results before ordering all objects. Size alone does not determine weight.
worked: Practice results: eraser heavier than leaf; stone heavier than eraser. Order: leaf, eraser, stone. These are stated results, not a rule for all stones.
play: Use three safe small objects and an adult-supervised balance. Predict, test, then change your order if evidence disagrees.
hint: Record the measured order. Objects with the same name need not have the same weight.

questions.prompt: In the practice results, which is lightest?
A is heavier than B. Which pan is lower?
Test and order three safe objects.

title: How much can it hold?
goal: Identify containers and order capacities.
look: Musa chooses a container for plant water. Does a taller container always hold more?
learn: Capacity is how much a container can hold. Measure with the same small cup each time. Use level cupfuls. A short wide container may hold more than a tall narrow one.
worked: Jug A holds 4 equal cups; B holds 6. B has greater capacity by 2 cups.
play: With adult help, use water or dry sand. Predict and measure three containers with one cup. Order from least to greatest capacity.
hint: Do not drink or taste activity contents. Prevent spills and use unbreakable containers.

questions.prompt: How many more cupfuls does B hold?

questions.answer: Suitable watertight jug, bucket or bottle.

questions.prompt: Compare two safe containers using one cup.
questions.answer: Recorded counts using a common cup unit.
So each unit has equal capacity.

title: Cover a surface
goal: Compare surface areas and recognise standard square units.
look: Zainab covers two cards with paper squares. What must she avoid between squares?
learn: Area measures flat surface coverage. Use equal squares without gaps or overlaps. More of the same squares means more area. A square centimetre is 1 cm on each side; write cm². A square metre is 1 m on each side; write m².
worked: Grid A has 3 rows of 4 squares: 12 square units. A card using 8 of the same squares has less area.
play: Cover two cards with equal paper squares. Record and compare. Use a ruler to make 1 cm squares when possible. Discuss which unit suits a book cover or floor.
hint: Area counts covering units, not distance around the edge. The diagram is not necessarily actual size.

questions.prompt: How many squares are in grid A?
Cards use 6 and 9 of the same squares. Which has more area?
Draw 2 rows of 3 equal squares. Count them.
Cover a card and record square units.
Why must comparison squares be equal?
questions.answer: Unequal unit sizes make counts unfair to compare.

title: Faces, edges and corners
goal: Count cube/cuboid features and recognise cylinder curvature.
look: Daniel turns a box. How can he avoid counting a corner twice?
learn: A polyhedron face is flat. An edge is where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner. Cube and cuboid each have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. A cylinder has a curved surface and two flat circular faces.
worked: Mark box corners with tabs. Count 4 on one end and 4 on the other: 8 vertices.
play: Explore a cube and non-cube box. Tab faces, edges and corners as you count. Compare with a cylinder and sphere. Find examples at home or school.
hint: Describe curved surfaces rather than extending polyhedron edge conventions to curved solids.

questions.prompt: Which has curvature: cube or cylinder?
Name a cylinder model at home.
How can you avoid recounting box edges?
questions.answer: Mark edges, or count four top, four bottom and four joining edges.

title: Triangles and square corners
goal: Name flat shapes and recognise right angles.
look: Amina folds a paper corner. Which corners in the room match it?
learn: A triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners. A right angle is a square corner. Squares and rectangles each have 4 right angles. A triangle may have one right angle, but need not.
worked: A rectangle stays a rectangle when turned. Fit a folded paper square corner against its corner to test the angle.
play: Trace circle, square, rectangle and triangle shapes. Sort by sides and right angles. Use a paper square corner to test.
hint: Not every triangle corner is a right angle. Use varied triangle shapes.

questions.prompt: How many right angles in a rectangle?
Draw a triangle with one right angle.
questions.answer: Three-sided shape with one square corner.

questions.prompt: Name a shape with 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.
How do triangle and rectangle differ?
questions.answer: Triangle has 3 sides; rectangle has 4 and four right angles.

title: Collect, group and arrange
goal: Collect information and organise groups and arrays.
look: Musa asks which of three games friends prefer. How can he record one choice per child?
learn: Choose a question and categories. Record one answer per person. Group matching answers. Place one counter per response in an array of aligned rows.
worked: Invented choices: ball, skipping, ball, clapping, ball, skipping. Counts: ball 3; skipping 2; clapping 1. Total 6.
play: Use the invented choices or a voluntary class question. Put a counter in its category for each answer. Align rows to compare counts.
hint: Avoid sensitive questions. Total counters must equal total responses.

questions.prompt: Draw labelled rows of 3, 2 and 1 dots.
Why one choice per child for this question?
questions.answer: Each participant is counted once, making counts comparable.
